text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday he saw a "genuine breakthrough" in Russian ties with Ukraine after years of tension between the two ex-Soviet states.
Yeltsin is scheduled to arrive in Kiev on Friday afternoon and is expected sign a treaty with Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Saturday.

After a two-hour briefing by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin at his country residence outside Moscow, the Kremlin press service said Yeltsin was satisfied with agreements the premier had signed in Kiev on Wednesday.
"These, and other accords, lay the foundation for the conclusion of a 'grand treaty' on friendship and cooperation between Russia and Ukraine," the Kremlin said in a statement.
"Its text is ready for signing during the forthcoming visit of the Russian president."
Similar visits have been planned and cancelled six times in as many years as the two former Soviet states have struggled to resolve a variety of problems.

The agreements reached by Chernomyrdin, notably on leasing facilities at Ukraine's Sevastopol port for Russian ships in the former Soviet Black Sea fleet, seem to have removed the remaining obstacles to an overall bilateral treaty, however.

"B.N. Yeltsin believes the signing of such a solid packet of documents between Russia and Ukraine should create a genuine breakthrough in their bilateral relations and give a response to many questions which have long stirred up public opinion in both countries and complicated their cooperation," the Kremlin said.
Chernomyrdin reached the accords in talks with Kuchma and Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko.

The documents resolve disputes between the Slav neighbours and biggest successor states of the Soviet Union. They were the second foreign policy breakthrough for Moscow this week, after the signing of the NATO-Russia Founding Act in Paris on Tuesday.
Under the deal, Ukraine will lease its naval base at Sevastopol in the Crimea to Russia for 20 years. Russia will keep the bulk of the Soviet Black Sea fleet at the base.
The deal did not go down well among the Russian opposition.
"You need a single navy to be able to cover our common Black Sea borders," communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said.
"This decision will worsen the situation, and will not increase Russia's or Ukraine's defence capability."
Chernomyrdin also covered Kiev's repayment of debt to Russia for oil and gas and compensation to Ukraine for nuclear missiles taken to Russia after the end of the Soviet Union.

Russian First Deputy Foreign Minister Boris Pastukhov said on Thursday Russia would pay rent totalling $98 to $100 million annually to Ukraine for the lease at Sevastopol. Part of the rent would be taken out of Ukraine's debts for oil and gas to Russia, which he said amounted to $526 million.
Ukrainian Deputy Foreign Minister Kostyantyn Hryshchenko said Kiev's debt to Russia had been restructured. "The issue of our state debt to Russia is closed," he told reporters.

Following Russia's deal with NATO, which responded to Moscow's opposition to NATO's planned expansion into eastern Europe by giving Russia a say in its affairs, Ukraine initialled its own accord with the western alliance.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko initialled the deal in the Portuguese town of Sintra. It gives Kiev the right to call for "consultations" with NATO if it feels threatened. The charter will be signed at a NATO summit in Madrid in July.
